title: Leveling the Playing Field: Attention Mitigates the Effects of Intelligence on Memory e-on-memory/ -- original paper:
author: Craig Barton
summary: This Tips for Teachers research summary covers Markant and Amso's study of how different attentional mechanisms shape memory encoding in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17. Using a spatial cueing paradigm, the researchers compared simple orienting (facilitation) against a more demanding mechanism called inhibition of return, which combines target selection with active suppression of competing information. The headline finding is that engaging suppression during learning substantially boosted recognition memory, and did so specifically for participants with lower IQ scores — when only basic orienting was engaged, IQ was the dominant predictor of memory performance, but suppression closed much of that gap. In other words, the quality of attention, not just the presence of it, determined how well information was encoded: simply looking at the same target for the same amount of time did not guarantee equal learning. Barton frames the finding as a potential equity lever, since a teaching approach that deliberately trains students to filter out distraction alongside focusing on relevant material could narrow achievement gaps tied to underlying cognitive differences. The authors are candid that the sample was drawn from a 'highly functioning' population and call for replication with children of lower IQ before drawing firm classroom conclusions.
points: Attentional suppression — actively filtering out irrelevant information, not just orienting toward the target — significantly boosted memory encoding, especially for participants with lower IQ scores.
When only basic orienting (facilitation) was engaged, IQ was the primary predictor of memory performance; suppression counteracted much of that IQ-driven gap, functioning as a potential equalizer.

Time-on-task alone did not predict learning — students who spent equal time looking at material encoded it unequally depending on which attentional mechanism (facilitation vs. suppression) was engaged.

The practical implication for teachers is to design tasks that require students to both focus on relevant information and actively suppress distractions, rather than simply directing attention toward a target.

The authors flag a key caution: the sample was 'highly functioning,' so the equity-levelling effect needs replication in children with a broader range of IQ, including lower scores, before being treated as classroom-ready.
quotes: This study explores how attention influences memory encoding in children and adolescents, specifically examining the impact of different attentional mechanisms.
Their findings indicate that engaging suppression during learning significantly enhances recognition memory, even counteracting the effects of individual differences in intelligence (IQ).

When only basic orienting was present, IQ was the primary predictor of memory performance, but suppression mechanisms proved crucial for boosting memory accuracy, particularly for participants with lower IQs.
Engaging selection via suppression is particularly impactful because it counteracts individual differences in intelligence.

The study found that simply spending the same amount of time looking at target items did not guarantee equal encoding efficacy; the underlying attentional mechanism (facilitation vs. suppression) was critical.
Specifically, we show that selection mechanisms involving suppression have the power to boost memory encoding, effectively counteracting individual differences in intelligence.
